title: Tokugawa Japan and the Closed Country

cards.h: Two centuries of peace behind closed doors
cards.b:
From 1603 to 1868 Japan was ruled by the Tokugawa shoguns. The country had almost no wars for over two hundred years. It limited foreign trade, but it also grew rich, urban and educated.

The Tokugawa period is one of the most surprising stories in world history. It shows that a state can shut the door and still build a rich culture.

In 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu won the battle of Sekigahara against rival warlords. He took the title of shogun in 1603 and set up a government in Edo, a fishing village that became a great city.

The shogun ruled through the daimyo, the regional lords. He kept them in line with a system of hostages, rules and inspections, which kept the peace for many generations.

cards.h: Edo: a city of a million
cards.b:
Edo, now Tokyo, grew to about a million people by the 1700s, making it one of the largest cities in the world. The daimyo had to spend time in Edo under the system called sankin-kōtai, or alternate attendance. Their families stayed there as hostages.

The system drove the building of roads, inns and castles. It also filled Edo with merchants, craftsmen and entertainers, who created a lively urban culture.

Engelbert Kaempfer (1651–1716)

A German doctor who worked for the Dutch East India Company, Kaempfer visited Japan in 1690 and 1692. He wrote a detailed history of the country, which was published in English in 1727.

His account gave Europe much of its knowledge of Japan for a long time, though it is shaped by the views of a visitor.
The shogunate ended in 1868, when samurai from the south restored imperial rule. The Meiji era then began.

cards.h: Shimabara and the fear of Christianity
cards.b:
In 1637 and 1638, Christian peasants and former samurai rose in revolt at Shimabara. The shogun's army crushed them, killing many. The revolt led the government to see Christianity as a threat and to ban missionaries.

Portuguese traders were expelled in 1639. The Dutch were allowed to stay, but only on the small artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki harbour.

Many people think that Japan closed its doors entirely from the 1600s until the arrival of Commodore Perry in 1853. The word "sakoku", or closed country, is often used for that picture.

Historians argue the picture is too simple. The term sakoku was coined only in 1801 by the scholar Shizuki Tadao. Trade continued through Dejima, Chinese merchants at Nagasaki, Korea through Tsushima and the Ryukyu islands through the Satsuma domain.

Through Dejima, Japanese scholars learned about Dutch medicine, astronomy and maps. This study was called rangaku, or Dutch learning. In 1774 a team translated a Dutch anatomy text into Japanese, the Kaitai Shinsho, which shows how serious the work was.

Dutch learning helped Japan prepare for the wave of Western power in the 1800s. It also made Japanese doctors and scholars among the best informed in East Asia.

During the peace, samurai became officials and scholars more than soldiers. Neo-Confucian ideas taught order, loyalty and education, and they shaped how the shogunate governed.

Historians argue whether the peace made Japan a stable, well-run state or a rigid society held back by its own rules. Both views have force. The peace did produce high literacy and a huge book trade.

Woodblock prints, kabuki theatre and popular novels grew up in Edo and Osaka. The woodblock prints of artists like Hokusai and Hiroshige, from the 1800s, were among the most famous images of Japan.

Literacy spread among townspeople, and the Edo book market was one of the largest in the world. Culture was no longer limited to the court.

The Dutch carried Japanese silver and copper to Asia, and some of it reached India. They used it to buy Indian cotton textiles on the Coromandel and Bengal coasts.

So Japanese metal financed Indian weaving, and Indian cloth then went back to Japan. The Tokugawa period shows how a closed country was still part of a global trade system.

Five things to remember
  1. Sekigahara in 1600 led to Tokugawa rule.
  2. The shogun ruled from Edo, which grew to about a million people.
  3. Shimabara (1637–1638) led to a ban on Christianity.
  4. The Dutch traded from Dejima.
  5. The shogunate ended in 1868.
Think about it
  • Can peace be a sign of strength for a state?
  • Was sakoku a policy, or a name given later?
